catalog_quote: Phonologically, Bilinarra and Ngarinyman are typical Pama-Nyungan languages. They have stops and nasals which have five corresponding places of articulation (bilabial, apico-alveolar, retroflex, palatal and velar), three laterals (apico-alveolar, retroflex, palatal), two rhotics (trill/flap and retroflex continuant), two semivowels (bilabial and palatal) and three vowels (a, i, u). Combinations of semivowels and vowels produce diphthong-like sounds. Like most Pama-Nyungan languages, Bilinarra and Ngarinyman are notable because they do not have fricatives or a voicing contrast between stops. Stress is word initial, and syllables pattern CV, CVC or CVCC.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (plain-text rendering of the saved DoBeS 'Jaminjungan and Eastern Ngumpin' Languages page; HTML metadata: canonicalhttps://dobes.mpi.nl/projects/jaminjung/languages/,datePublished 2013-09-23, dateModified 2013-11-14). Line 112 is the heading 'Bilinarra and Ngarinyman'; line 114 is the phonology paragraph and reads exactly as quoted, ending 'Like most Pama-Nyungan languages, Bilinarra and Ngarinyman are notable because they do not have fricatives or a voicing contrast between stops. Stress is word initial, and syllables pattern CV, CVC or CVCC.' The report's '[..]' elides only the sentence 'Combinations of semivowels and vowels produce diphthong-like sounds.'; everything else is verba…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of the word in Ngarinyman and Bilinarra (as in neighbouring Gurindji). Supporting first-hand remark: McConvell 1980:78 (PL A-59), on Gurindji/Bilinara/Mudbura, 'A separate word would normally have primary or at least secondary stress on the initial syllable', used as a wordhood test for the clitic complex.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in the DoBeS sketch. McConvell 1980 (pp. 57, 78, 103) mentions secondary stresses on certain link/clitic syllables in the Eastern Ngumpin clitic complex; the sister-language description for Gurindji (Ennever et al. 2017:3) reports secondary stress on suffix-initial syllables with alternation otherwise, but that is not stated for Ngarinyman in any source opened.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a brief web sketch by the documentation team; no discussion of phrase-level prosody or citation forms. The fuller first-hand treatment is Meakins & Nordlinger 2014 sec. 2.2.6 'Stress' (pp. 65-66, Bilinarra dialect), not accessible here.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted DoBeS statement is made jointly for 'Bilinarra and Ngarinyman'. Glottolog ngar1235 'Ngarinman' subsumes Bilinarra as a dialect (bili1250) alongside Eastern Ngarinman (east2376) and Wurlayi (wurl1241); the fuller grammar (Meakins & Nordlinger 2014) describes the Bilinarra dialect specifically (Pigeon Hole/Yarralin), while Jones 1996 and Jones et al. 2019 describe Ngarinyman proper. McConvell 1980's remark covers 'Bilinara' together with Gurindji (guri1247) and Mudburra (mudb1240).
